newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya holds second round of parliamentary poll.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya holds second round of parliamentary poll.

text.p: Chechens went to the polls on Saturday for a second round of voting to choose a new parliament that will help steer the breakaway region through the postwar period of reconstruction.
Polling was taking place in nearly 60 districts across the tiny, mountainous territory where no candidate won a clear majority in the first round on January 27, Itar-Tass news agency said.

President Aslan Maskhadov, who formally took office on Wednesday after easily beating his rivals for the top post last month, plans to head the new government, dispensing with a prime minister, Tass said.
It added that Maskhadov, who is also commander-in-chief, also intended to take over the defence portfolio.

Maskhadov, who led the separatist guerrilla struggle against Russian troops during 21 months of bloody fighting, is expected in the coming days to select his new cabinet, which will likely include other prominent rebels.

The gently-spoken, pragmatic Maskhadov, a former Soviet artillery colonel, promised during his inauguration address to strengthen Chechnya's dominant Moslem religion and to fight a crime wave sweeping the shattered region.
He also made clear that Chechnya saw itself as an independent state, despite its lack of international diplomatic recognition.
Moscow, fearing separatism elsewhere on its vast territories, insists the region remains part of the Russian Federation and will not discuss sovereignty for five years.
On Friday Russian President Boris Yeltsin urged Maskhadov to work for peace and, clearly cautioning him against secessionist moves, told him not to make any "one-sided decisions".
Yeltsin said Maskhadov should concentrate on sorting out problems within Chechnya, which also contains ethnic Russians.
A new commission headed by Ivan Rybkin, secretary of Russia's Security Council, will draw up plans in the coming weeks aimed at clarifying relations between Moscow and Chechnya.
Despite their strongly pro-independence rhetoric, Chechnya's rebel leaders desperately need Russian assistance to rebuild their economy.
